title: Paired texts: cooling a city street
bodyMd:
**Text 1**

Urban climatologist Priya Raghavan measured air temperature at sixty sites across a mid-sized city during a July heat wave. Streets lined with mature trees averaged 2.8 degrees Celsius cooler at midday than treeless streets a few blocks away. Raghavan argues that widening the street-tree canopy is therefore the most cost-effective protection the city can offer its residents during extreme heat, because trees draw no electricity and keep cooling the air year after year once they are established.

**Text 2**

Engineer Tobias Lindqvist does not dispute that tree-shaded streets are cooler at midday. He notes, however, that his own overnight readings found no difference between canopied and treeless streets after 10 p.m., because dense canopy traps the heat that pavement releases at night. Since the city's heat-related hospital admissions cluster in the hours before dawn, Lindqvist contends that reflective pavement, which keeps heat from being stored in the first place, deserves at least equal investment.
accessibilityText: Two short paired texts. Text 1: urban climatologist Priya Raghavan measured temperature at sixty city sites in a July heat wave and found tree-lined streets averaged 2.8 degrees Celsius cooler at midday than nearby treeless streets; she argues widening the tree canopy is the most cost-effective heat protection because trees use no electricity and keep working once established. Text 2: engineer Tobias Lindqvist does not dispute the midday cooling, but his overnight readings after 10 p.m. found no difference between canopied and treeless streets, because dense canopy traps the heat pavement releases at night; since heat-related hospital admissions cluster before dawn, he argues reflective pavement deserves at least equal investment.

provenance.notes: Original paired texts written for this item bank. Both researchers, both studies and all figures are invented.
